title: Multiply Mostly-Zero Matrices
statement:
You get two integer matrices: a with m rows and k columns, and b with k rows and n columns. Return their product, an m × n matrix where cell [i][j] is the sum of a[i][t] · b[t][j] over every t.

Most entries of both matrices are zero. A good answer spends its time on the nonzero entries instead of multiplying zeros by things.

examples.why: Row 0 of a only has the 2 in column 0, so it only picks up row 0 of b, times 2. Row 1 only has the −1 in column 2, so it picks up row 2 of b, negated.
An all-zero matrix wipes everything out. A sparse solution does no multiplications at all here.
A 1 × 2 times a 2 × 1 gives a single cell: 1·3 + 2·4.

constraints: a has k columns and b has k rows
hints: Write out the textbook triple loop. Which of its multiplications are guaranteed to add nothing?
Reorder the loops to i, t, j. Now the middle loop reads a single entry a[i][t]. What can you do when it is zero?
For the sparsest inputs, first list the nonzero entries of each row of b once. Then each nonzero a[i][t] only touches the nonzero entries of row t of b.

explain.intuition:
The usual triple loop computes every cell as a dot product, so it multiplies zeros all day. Flip the order of the loops: for row i of a, walk its entries a[i][t], and for each one add a[i][t] · b[t][j] into result[i][j] for every j. Same sum, different order.

The payoff is that now a single value a[i][t] guards a whole inner loop. If it is zero, skip the loop entirely. Precompute the nonzero entries of each row of b too, and the work drops to roughly the number of nonzero pairs that actually meet. It is the same idea as a virtual DOM diff that only touches the nodes that changed.
steps: Create an m × n result filled with zeros.
For each row t of b, collect the list of (j, b[t][j]) pairs where the value is nonzero.
For each i and each t with a[i][t] ≠ 0, loop over the nonzero pairs of row t of b and add a[i][t] · value into result[i][j].
pitfalls: Getting the shapes wrong: the result is m × n, where m is the row count of a and n is the column count of b, not k.
Skipping a cell because the partial sum became zero. Positive and negative products can cancel, as in [[1, -1]], and the cell must still exist as 0.
Building the nonzero list of b by column inside the loop. It must be precomputed once, or the skipping saves nothing.

complexity.time: O(m·k + k·n + number of nonzero pairs that meet), O(m·k·n) at worst

solutions.title: Textbook triple loop
solutions.idea: Compute every cell as the dot product of a row of a and a column of b, zeros included.

solutions.title: Skip zeros using nonzero lists
solutions.idea: Loop in i, t, j order so one entry of a guards a whole inner loop, and only visit the nonzero entries of each row of b.

followups: The matrices are too big to store as 2D arrays, only as lists of (row, column, value). How do you multiply them?
You multiply the same a by many different b matrices. What would you precompute?
